title: The Role of Estrogen and Its Receptors in Brain Development and Their Long‐Term Effects
content:
Estrogen signaling shapes brain development through receptor-, cell-, region-, and stage-specific mechanisms. Endogenous estrogens, locally synthesized estradiol, and exogenous estrogenic exposures interact with androgenic pathways in a species-dependent manner to regulate neuronal differentiation, synaptic organization, glial function, and neuroendocrine circuit formation. Perturbations in steroid signaling during sensitive developmental windows may produce persistent neuroendocrine, metabolic, behavioral, and neuropsychiatric consequences.


ABSTRACT

Estrogens are a class of steroid hormones that participate not only in reproduction and sexual differentiation but also in brain development. The major endogenous estrogens include estrone (E1), 17β-estradiol (E2), and estriol (E3), whose relative abundance and biological sources vary across sex and life stage. During fetal and early postnatal development, estrogenic signaling is sensitive to both intrinsic physiological conditions and extrinsic environmental factors. Through estrogen receptor (ER)-mediated signaling, endogenous estrogens regulate neuronal migration, differentiation, and synaptic plasticity, thereby influencing brain morphology, functional development, and sexual differentiation. Dysregulated estrogen signaling may alter the development of sexually differentiated brain regions and thereby contribute to sex-related differences in brain function and disease vulnerability. This review summarizes the distribution and expression patterns of estrogen and its receptors in the brain, elucidates the role of endogenous estrogen and ERs in neurodevelopment, and examines the impact of exogenous estrogenic and endocrine-disrupting exposures on brain maturation. Together, these findings provide a framework for understanding how estrogen signaling contributes to neurodevelopment and its long-term outcomes.
